title: More than 800,000 hours of sewage spills in Wales last year, report claims
summary: It is equivalent to a sewage discharge happening every five minutes, according to campaigners.
text: Sewage spills in Wales exceeded 800,000 hours last year, report claims - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat Wales Wales Politics Wales Business North West North East Mid South West South East Cymru Local News More than 800,000 hours of sewage spills in Wales last year, report claims Image source, Getty Images Image caption, There were more than 100,000 sewage discharges from Welsh water companies in 2025 By Dan Moffat BBC Wales Published 8 October 2026 New figures show sewage was released into rivers, lakes and the sea around Wales for more than 800,000 hours last year. The charity Surfers Against Sewage, which has analysed data from Wales' water companies, said there were more than 100,000 sewage discharges in 2025 - or one every five minutes. The figures are down on the year before when sewage was discharged for more than 970,000 hours. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it had strengthened its approach as regulators through increased monitoring and tighter guidance, and had overseen "significant programmes of environmental investment" by water companies. Surfers Against Sewage said part of the reason for the drop was the dry weather seen during the summer last year, but underinvestment and a lack of enforcement remained an issue. In its annual assessment, it said since 2019 it had received 992 reports of sickness in Wales caused by sewage, with 215 of those coming in 2025. It said the impact of those sickness reports led to more than 2,200 days off work. According to the charity, sewage was discharged into Wales' designated bathing waters for a total of 35,669 hours over the year. At Llyn Padarn, Gwynedd, despite the lake's designated bathing water being classified as "excellent" for water quality, discharges lasted 1,614 hours. Rules allow a limited discharge of sewage in periods of excess rain, but environmental groups remain concerned the levels pose a threat to wildlife and a health risk to swimmers. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Surfers Against Sewage has been campaigning for better water quality across the UK Giles Bristow, chief executive of Surfers Against Sewage, said last year's figures equated to a discharge every five minutes, which he called a "shocking statistic". He pointed to 90 places that authorities have said are good places to swim, but said they'd "been impacted by over 4,000 hours of sewage pollution". "It's a really terrible picture that we're seeing of continued underinvestment and a lack of enforcement to ensure that this isn't happening," he added. "People's lives and their health are being put at risk when they go to enjoy these amazing places." Welsh Water said it would invest a record £2.5bn over the next four years, and understood the concerns about sewage discharge. "We take our responsibility to protect these waters seriously and recognise that we need to improve," it said. "In line with Welsh government policy, we are prioritising the overflows causing the greatest environmental harm." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The Welsh government says it is "taking full control of water in Wales" Hafren Dyfrdwy - which operates in mid and north-east Wales - said it was "working tirelessly" to reduce the average number of spills but "we know more needs to be done". "Which is why we're investing £11m at our storm overflows to reduce spills to fewer than 20 a year by 2030," it added. The Welsh government said it was "taking full control of water in Wales" and would "apply the polluter-pays principle, including prosecuting serious and persistent offenders". "Water reform demonstrates how Wales and the UK can work together to strengthen and simplify devolution, while keeping effective cross-border cooperation," a spokesperson added. Laura Anne Jones MS, Reform spokesperson for Food, Farming and Agriculture, called the most recent figures a "disgrace". "Our waterways and beaches are some of the finest in the world, and everyone in Wales deserves to enjoy them unpolluted," she said. "Reform value our natural resources, we would review the current EU law and introduce a Welsh Rivers Act to protect our beautiful rivers and beaches." The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said water companies must "take responsibility" for record levels of sewage pollution. It added: "Our strengthened Water Bill will deliver cleaner waters, stronger accountability and will create a powerful new regulator to hold companies to account."
